newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanian students hail soldier who shot Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Jordanian students hail soldier who shot Israelis.

text.p: More than 1,000 Jordanian university students marched on Sunday in support of a soldier sentenced to life imprisonment for killing seven Israeli schoolgirls.
Waving banners against Jordan's peace accord with Israel and holding up copies of the Moslem holy book, the Koran, students chanted for the soldier, army private Ahmed Daqamsa.
"Don't fear prison, Ahmed our hero. Even if they say you are mad," the marchers sang as dozens of police looked on. "Hold your head up high, We don't want to see your eyes weeping."

Daqamsa was sentenced by a military court on Saturday to life imprisonment with hard labour for shooting the Israeli girls, aged between 11 and 13, while they were on an outing in March to the patch of borderland where he was posted.
The court said Daqamsa was mentally disturbed and incapable of planning the attack in advance, but it rejected defence arguments that he was provoked while at prayer by the girls.
"He stained his military honour with the blood of the innocent girls, who were promised safe entry into this restored Arab land," military judge Mamoun Khasawneh said.

Daqamsa was stationed on a small patch of northern border land returned to Jordanian sovereignty but leased to Israel under the 1994 peace accord, which ended a decades-long formal state of war between the two countries.

The area, called Baqoura in Jordan, was a popular picnic site for Israelis who named it the Island of Peace. Jordan says it was "liberated" by the treaty but the opposition say it was meekly surrendered to Jordan's enemy of 46 years.
King Hussein, champion of the peace treaty with Israel, rebuked his army for not shooting Daqamsa dead on the spot and flew to Jerusalem to grieve with families of the dead girls.
But opponents of the peace rallied round Daqamsa, saying Israelis who killed Arabs were treated more leniently and the soldier was punished to protect close ties with Israel.
"This was a political trial right from the beginning," said opposition member of parliament Toujan Feisal.

"Politicians had bet his mental state gave a legitimate way out for his acquittal," the opposition Hadath paper said on Sunday, comparing Daqamsa to Israeli soldier Naom Friedman who fired on Palestinians in the West Bank town of Hebron and was confined to a psychiatric hospital instead of facing charges.
Daqamsa's supporters during the trial included prominent opponents of the peace treaty, including parliamentary deputies, a professional union leader and a former prime minister.
Women students in white headscarves filed past the gates of Jordan University on Sunday holding copies of the Koran and waving black flags with Islamic slogans.
Inside the university students burnt a cardboard image of Israel's flag while student leaders condemned the Jewish state.

"We have reached the end. They have violated our Koran and cursed our prophet," one student leader said in reference to posters put up in Hebron showing the prophet Mohammad as a pig. "Stand up against this failed peace process," he shouted.

Unease in Jordan at the peace treaty has been fuelled by the absence of material benefits promised from the accord, and by the stalemate in Palestinian self-rule talks since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power last year.
